paragraphs: After plain experience of the ineffectiveness of the existing federal government, you are called upon to deliberate on a new Constitution for the United States of America. The subject speaks to its own importance, for its consequences reach nothing less than the existence of the UNION, the safety and welfare of the parts that compose it, and the fate of an empire that is in many respects the most interesting in the world. It has often been remarked that it seems to have been reserved for the people of this country, by their conduct and example, to decide an important question: whether societies of men are truly capable of establishing good government through reflection and choice, or whether they are forever destined to depend on accident and force for their political constitutions. If there is any truth in this remark, the crisis we have now reached may rightly be regarded as the era in which that decision is to be made. A wrong choice of the part we shall act may, in this view, deserve to be considered the general misfortune of mankind.

This thought adds the motives of philanthropy to those of patriotism, and heightens the concern that every thoughtful and good person must feel about the outcome. It will be fortunate if our choice is guided by a sound estimate of our true interests, undisturbed and unbiased by considerations unconnected with the public good. But this is more to be ardently wished than seriously expected. The plan offered for our deliberation affects too many particular interests and makes changes in too many local institutions for its discussion not to involve a variety of matters foreign to its merits, and of views, passions and prejudices that do little to help the discovery of truth.

Among the most formidable obstacles the new Constitution will have to meet, we can readily pick out two. The first is the obvious interest of a certain class of men in every State to resist any change that might risk a reduction of the power, pay, and standing of the offices they hold under the State establishments. The second is the corrupted ambition of another class of men, who will either hope to raise themselves through the confusions of their country, or will flatter themselves with better prospects of advancement from the division of the empire into several separate confederacies than from its union under one government.

It is not my design, however, to dwell on observations of this kind. I am well aware that it would be dishonest to put down the opposition of any set of men indiscriminately to selfish or ambitious motives, merely because their situations might expose them to suspicion. Fairness obliges us to admit that even such men may be moved by upright intentions. And it cannot be doubted that much of the opposition that has appeared, or may yet appear, will spring from sources that are blameless, if not respectable: the honest errors of minds led astray by preconceived jealousies and fears. So numerous and so powerful are the causes that give a false bias to the judgment that we often see wise and good men on the wrong side, as well as the right side, of questions of the first importance to society. This fact, if properly attended to, would be a lesson in moderation for those who are most firmly persuaded that they are right in any controversy. A further reason for caution could be drawn from the reflection that we are not always sure that those who advocate the truth are moved by purer principles than their opponents. Ambition, greed, personal animosity, party opposition, and many other motives no more praiseworthy than these are apt to operate on those who support the right side of a question as well as on those who oppose it. Even if there were no such reasons for moderation, nothing could be more ill-judged than that intolerant spirit which has at all times characterized political parties. For in politics, as in religion, it is equally absurd to try to make converts by fire and sword. Heresies in either can rarely be cured by persecution.

And yet, however just these views will be allowed to be, we already have sufficient signs that this case will go as all earlier cases of great national debate have gone. A torrent of angry and malicious passions will be let loose. Judging from the conduct of the opposing parties, we shall be led to conclude that each hopes to prove the justice of its opinions, and to increase the number of its converts, by the loudness of its declamations and the bitterness of its invective. An enlightened zeal for the energy and effectiveness of government will be branded as the offspring of a temperament fond of despotic power and hostile to the principles of liberty. An over-scrupulous jealousy of danger to the rights of the people, which is more commonly a fault of the head than of the heart, will be represented as mere pretense and artifice, the stale bait for popularity at the expense of the public good. On the one hand, it will be forgotten that jealousy is the usual companion of love, and that the noble enthusiasm of liberty is apt to be infected with a spirit of narrow and illiberal distrust. On the other hand, it will be just as readily forgotten that the vigor of government is essential to the security of liberty; that, in the view of a sound and well-informed judgment, their interests can never be separated; and that a dangerous ambition more often lurks behind the specious mask of zeal for the rights of the people than behind the forbidding appearance of zeal for the firmness and effectiveness of government. History will teach us that the former has proved a much more certain road to despotism than the latter, and that, of those men who have overturned the liberties of republics, the greatest number began their careers by paying servile court to the people: they began as demagogues and ended as tyrants.

In these observations, my fellow-citizens, I have had in view to put you on your guard against all attempts, from whatever quarter, to influence your decision, on a matter of the utmost importance to your welfare, by any impressions other than those that result from the evidence of truth. You will no doubt also have gathered, from the general drift of them, that they come from a source not unfriendly to the new Constitution. Yes, my countrymen, I own to you that, after giving it careful consideration, I am clearly of the opinion that it is in your interest to adopt it. I am convinced that this is the safest course for your liberty, your dignity, and your happiness. I do not pretend to a reserve I do not feel. I will not amuse you with an appearance of deliberation when I have already decided. I frankly acknowledge my convictions to you, and I will freely lay before you the reasons on which they are founded. A consciousness of good intentions disdains ambiguity. I shall not, however, multiply professions on this point. My motives must remain in the keeping of my own breast. My arguments will be open to all, and may be judged by all. They shall at least be offered in a spirit that will not disgrace the cause of truth.
I propose, in a series of papers, to discuss the following interesting subjects:

THE USEFULNESS OF THE UNION TO YOUR POLITICAL PROSPERITY. THE INSUFFICIENCY OF THE PRESENT CONFEDERATION TO PRESERVE THAT UNION. THE NECESSITY OF A GOVERNMENT AT LEAST EQUALLY ENERGETIC WITH THE ONE PROPOSED, TO ATTAIN THIS OBJECT. THE CONFORMITY OF THE PROPOSED CONSTITUTION TO THE TRUE PRINCIPLES OF REPUBLICAN GOVERNMENT. ITS RESEMBLANCE TO YOUR OWN STATE CONSTITUTION. And lastly, THE ADDITIONAL SECURITY WHICH ITS ADOPTION WILL GIVE TO THE PRESERVATION OF THAT KIND OF GOVERNMENT, TO LIBERTY, AND TO PROPERTY.
As this discussion proceeds, I shall endeavor to give a satisfactory answer to every objection that has appeared and that may seem to have any claim to your attention.

It may perhaps be thought needless to offer arguments to prove the usefulness of the UNION. It is a point, no doubt, deeply engraved on the hearts of the great body of the people in every State, and one that, it might be imagined, has no opponents. But the fact is that we already hear it whispered in the private circles of those who oppose the new Constitution that the thirteen States are too large for any general system, and that we must of necessity resort to separate confederacies of distinct portions of the whole.(1) This doctrine will in all probability be gradually spread until it has enough followers to support an open avowal of it. For nothing can be more evident, to those who are able to take a broad view of the subject, than that the alternative is between adopting the new Constitution and breaking up the Union. It will therefore be useful to begin by examining the advantages of that Union, and the certain evils and probable dangers to which every State would be exposed by its dissolution. This shall accordingly be the subject of my next address.
1. The same idea, tracing the arguments to their consequences, is put forward in several of the recent publications against the new Constitution.
